title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Wichita, KS: Six-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Wichita aerospace, refinery, machinery and pipeline welders: corporate on site, online at your pace, or one-to-one.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Wichita, Kansas: Six Days for Aerospace, Refinery and Manufacturing Welding Inspectors
html:
Wichita calls itself the Air Capital of the World, and most people picture rivets, fasteners and composites when they think of its plants. Welding still runs right through the regional economy: in tooling, fixtures and ground support equipment for the aircraft lines, in tubular and exhaust parts for light aircraft, in the refinery at El Dorado, in the column internals designed in the city, in farm and construction machinery, and in the pipelines that cross Kansas. For Kansas welders aiming at the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination, Atlantis NDT offers a six-day (6-day) preparation course that works through Part A Fundamentals, Part B Practical and Part C Code Application. Wichita candidates can take it as corporate delivery at their employer's site, as online study at their own pace, or as six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor. AWS administers the examination, rules on eligibility and grants the certification; the Atlantis course prepares you and certifies no one. There is no Atlantis classroom in Wichita, and the company's offices are in Houston, Texas and Hyderabad, India. To scope a course for one person or a team, send a Wichita CWI enquiry.

How the six-day course reaches Wichita

The outline is identical in all three formats. Days one and two cover Part A ground: processes, terms, joint design, welding symbols, metallurgy, testing, discontinuities, safety and ethics. Day three is practical preparation with gauges and documents, day four is spent working inside the code book you will choose, day five is timed practice papers, and day six revisits weak topics and walks through exam logistics. The full breakdown sits on the AWS CWI exam prep page.

  • Corporate. An aerostructures supplier, tooling shop, refinery contractor or farm equipment plant can host the six days for a group of its staff. The practical day uses the plant's own gauges and welded parts, and the code work can follow the specification and code the group actually builds to.
  • Online. An individual gets a study plan built on the six-day outline, course materials, original practice questions and timed practice papers, with an instructor answering questions along the way. There are no class times to keep, so second and third shift workers study when they can.
  • One-to-one. One candidate books six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor, either online or in person at a location agreed when booking. It suits someone retaking a single part or a supervisor who needs focused help with a code book.

The practice material in every format is written by Atlantis against the subject areas AWS publishes. It is not drawn from any AWS examination, and AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed the course.

Is a CWI worth having in an aircraft town?

It is a fair question in Wichita. Most of an aluminum fuselage section or wing structure is joined with rivets, fasteners and bonding rather than fusion welds, and the inspectors on those lines spend their time on fastener installation, sealing and composite work. Welding sits around that core. Light aircraft use welded steel tube parts such as engine mounts, and exhaust components, ducts, brackets and fittings are welded too. Every assembly line also depends on a large volume of welded tooling, fixtures, jigs, stands and ground support equipment. Aerospace fusion welding is governed by customer specifications and by AWS D17.1, and the people who inspect it work on joint preparation, weld profile, discontinuity limits and paperwork.

The CWI is not a requirement for every aerospace inspection job, and requirements vary by employer and role. What it gives a Wichita inspector is portability. When aircraft build rates slow, the same person can move into refinery turnaround work, a farm equipment plant or a structural fabricator with a credential each of those employers recognises.

The aerospace employers

Boeing completed its acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems in December 2025, bringing Spirit's Wichita commercial operations, which build fuselages for the 737 program and major structures for the 767, 777 and 787, into Boeing. Spirit's defense business continues as Spirit Defense, a separately governed Boeing subsidiary. Textron Aviation, maker of Cessna and Beechcraft aircraft, is headquartered at Wichita's Eisenhower National Airport, where Bombardier also runs a major operation. The Greater Wichita Partnership lists Bell Flight and Airbus among the region's aerospace employers as well, and counts more than 350 regional suppliers, among them hundreds of precision machine, tool and die shops. Welding inspectors in this world often work for those suppliers and tool builders rather than on the final assembly lines.

Beyond aviation: refining, process equipment, machinery and pipelines

The refinery at El Dorado

Northeast of Wichita in Butler County, HF Sinclair's El Dorado refinery has a crude oil capacity of 135,000 barrels per day, and the company calls it one of the largest refineries in the Plains and Mid-continent region. Refinery piping is built and repaired under ASME B31.3 with procedures and welders qualified to Section IX, and turnarounds bring waves of contract welders, fitters and QC inspectors through the gate. For Wichita welders who follow that work, the ASME Part C option is the logical book.

Process equipment designed in the city

Wichita is home to Koch Industries, and Koch-Glitsch, a supplier of mass transfer equipment such as trays and packing for distillation columns, lists its main office here. Column internals end up inside refinery and chemical plant towers, which ties part of the local engineering economy to the same turnaround market as El Dorado.

Machinery, grain and fabrication across Kansas

The AWS Kansas Section's own tours give a picture of the rest of the market: Great Plains Manufacturing's construction equipment plant in Salina, a soybean crush facility near Cherryvale, a company building collaborative welding robots, and PKM Steel. Farm and construction machinery, grain handling equipment, trailers and structural steel are built across south-central Kansas. Much of it follows manufacturers' own standards, with AWS D1.1 often the structural reference behind them and AWS D1.2 where the parts are aluminum.

Pipelines across the state

Natural gas and liquids pipelines cross Kansas in every direction, and the Kansas Section has held an event at Southern Star Central Gas Pipeline's facility in Hesston. Pipeline construction, station work and repairs follow API 1104, the standard federal pipeline safety regulations incorporate for welding and weld acceptance.

Who hires welding inspectors around Wichita

  • Aerospace suppliers and tool builders. Machine shops, tooling companies and detail-part suppliers with welding cells need people who can inspect to customer specifications and D17.1-based requirements.
  • Ground support and test equipment makers. Stands, carts and fixtures are welded structures, usually built to D1.1 or D1.2 and checked before delivery to the aircraft plants.
  • Refinery and turnaround contractors. Mechanical contractors working at El Dorado and other Mid-continent plants staff QC with inspectors fluent in Section IX and B31.3.
  • Machinery and agricultural equipment manufacturers. High-volume production welding of frames and booms needs in-process inspection and audits of welder qualification.
  • Pipeline contractors and operators. Construction and integrity repair work across Kansas calls for API 1104 inspectors.
  • Structural fabricators and erectors. Commercial building, hospital, school and industrial projects in the metro bring D1.1 shop and field inspection.

Choosing a Part C book in Wichita

AWS lets every candidate choose the code for the open-book Part C. Its list covers AWS D1.1 for structural steel, API 1104 for pipelines, D1.2 for aluminum, D1.5 for bridges, D15.1 for railcars and locomotives, D17.1 for aerospace fusion welding, an ASME option combining Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, and an ISO option. Wichita is unusual because a fair share of candidates genuinely sit between two of them.

Where you inspectLikely bookNotes for Wichita candidates
Aerospace detail parts, engine mounts, exhaust and duct assembliesAWS D17.1Closest to aerospace fusion welding; your customer's specification still governs on the job
Refinery, chemical and power piping; vessel and exchanger shopsASME Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3The book for El Dorado and other Mid-continent turnaround work
Tooling, stands, machinery frames, buildingsAWS D1.1Prequalified joints, qualification and visual acceptance for steel structures
Aluminum structures, trailers, some ground equipmentAWS D1.2Worth considering if most of your welds are aluminum
Gas and liquids pipelines, compressor and pump stationsAPI 1104Welder and procedure qualification by destructive testing, plus acceptance standards

If you split your time between aerospace and industrial work, choose the book for the welds you expect to be accepting next year, not the ones you accepted last year. Whatever you pick, study the edition AWS names for the exam, which can trail the newest printing. Background: AWS D1.1, D1.1 weld acceptance criteria and API 1104.

The AWS Kansas Section

The AWS section that meets around Wichita is the Kansas Section, part of District 16. Its meetings move across south-central Kansas: a business meeting in Andover, just east of Wichita; a session at Southern Star Central Gas Pipeline in Hesston; an event at Galaxy Technologies in Winfield; a meeting at the Hutchinson Career and Technical Education Academy; and plant tours such as Great Plains Manufacturing in Salina. For a CWI candidate those evenings are worth the drive. You meet inspectors who have sat the exam recently, QC managers who know which employers are hiring, and people who can confirm the welding history you will list for AWS.

WSU Tech, NCAT and the Wichita welding pipeline

WSU Tech, the technical college linked to Wichita State University, teaches welding at the National Center for Aviation Training on North Webb Road. It offers an Associate of Applied Science in Welding Technology and Level 1 and Level 2 technical certificates. The program covers arc and resistance welding, brazing and soldering, cutting, high-energy beam and solid-state processes, plus ferrous and nonferrous materials, welding metallurgy, heat treating, structural design and codes. Students test for AWS welder qualifications, including D1.1 groove welds in the 3G and 4G positions, and the college describes itself as an AWS SENSE partner. Other Wichita welders come through high school career programs, company training and years in the shop.

For the CWI that schooling counts twice. An associate degree in a field AWS accepts can lower the experience requirement to two years, and completed trade courses to four, against five years for a high school diploma alone. And transcripts plus welder qualification records make the work history AWS asks for much easier to verify.

Sitting each part from Wichita

Your AWS confirmation carries an eligibility code. Quote it to Prometric to reserve seats for the two computer-based parts, Part A and Part C; AWS says Prometric has more than 450 centers worldwide, over 100 of them in the United States. The practical is scheduled separately, because AWS gives Part B only at its own seminar and examination locations, on dates it fixes. A Wichita candidate should expect that the nearest practical session may be in another city or state and plan time off and travel around it.

Know the shape of the exam before you plan your study. Fundamentals is 150 questions across processes, metallurgy, testing, symbols, safety, math and procedures. The practical pairs hands-on tasks using AWS equipment with 46 questions. Code Application asks roughly 50 to 65 questions with your book open. You need 72 percent or better on every part. AWS posts its examination fees on aws.org; the course is quoted separately on request, and the CWI exam budget guide helps with the rest of the planning.

Studying around build rates and refinery turnarounds

Aerospace production in Wichita rises and falls with build rates, and overtime follows. Refinery and pipeline work comes in turnaround and construction seasons. Online study fits both: do the fundamentals blocks when overtime eases, keep a tabbed code book at your bench or in your bag, and practise Part B measurements on scrap parts and test coupons with the gauges you use every day. Leave the timed practice papers for the weeks just before your Prometric booking, when exam pacing matters most. If a question comes up mid-shift, send it to the instructor and pick up the answer when you are next studying.

Corporate: six days inside a Wichita plant or shop

When a supplier, tooling company or machinery plant has several people to prepare, the six days can be delivered at its facility. An aerospace supplier can use its own welded assemblies and specification for the measurement and acceptance exercises, while a D1.1 shop works with its own frames and fixtures. Mixed groups are common in Wichita, so the code day can divide between D17.1, D1.1 and the ASME book. Dates can be planned around production commitments and customer audits. Each person still applies to AWS individually and must meet the experience and vision rules personally; the employer cannot file any part of that for them.

One-to-one sessions, online or in person

Six days of one-to-one sessions give a single candidate the instructor's full attention. Sessions can run online or in person at a location agreed when booking. Because nobody else is in the room, the time follows your weak spots: a composite technician moving into welding may need two full days on processes and metallurgy, while a veteran fabricator may need nearly all the time on code navigation. It is also a sensible choice after a failed part, since AWS reports scores by part and you can aim straight at the one you missed.

Eligibility and the eye examination

AWS sets the required years of welding-related experience by education. With a high school diploma it is five years; with a bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology it is one; associate degrees, engineering or technical coursework and trade courses sit in between, and less schooling means more years. Experience must be verifiable work on welded products, such as production, inspection or repair. The vision requirement is separate: an AWS Visual Acuity Record showing near vision of Jaeger J2 at 12 inches or more, corrected or not, and a color perception test, performed by an eye-care or medical professional within the time AWS allows before your exam. The full table is on the CWI exam prep course page. Candidates short of the years can look at the AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector (CAWI), which works under a CWI's supervision.

After the CWI in Wichita

AWS keeps a CWI valid for nine years, with renewal applications at three and six years and recertification at nine. From there, Wichita inspectors usually move one of three ways. Some stay in aerospace and become the welding specialist in a supplier's quality department. Some follow refinery and pipeline work and deepen their ASME or API 1104 knowledge, adding AWS endorsements as they go. And many add nondestructive testing, because a CWI who can also perform penetrant, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing is more useful to a small shop. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its NDT technicians once training and logged experience are complete, and aerospace employers add their customers' requirements on top. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A-based training; see NDT training in Wichita, aerospace NDT training in Wichita, PT Level 2 training and visual testing. The AWS Senior CWI is the step for people who run inspection programs; see the Senior CWI pathway. To weigh the CWI against other credentials, read CWI requirements and career value.

Related pages and a Wichita quote

Nearby CWI exam prep pages: Oklahoma City, Kansas City, Tulsa and Omaha. To rehearse inspection steps in a browser, see Practical NDT for Wichita.

For a quote, tell us which format suits you (corporate, online or one-to-one), how many people want to prepare, an outline of each person's schooling and welding work, and which Part C book each is leaning toward. For delivery at your plant, include the address, the gauges and sample parts you can provide, and any build-rate peaks or audits to avoid. Send it through the Wichita CWI enquiry form.

faq.q: Does Atlantis teach the CWI course in a Wichita classroom?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Wichita. Candidates take the six-day course as corporate delivery at their employer's site, as online study at their own pace with instructor support, or as six days of one-to-one sessions online or in person at an agreed location. See the outline.

AWS. The American Welding Society administers every part of the examination, reviews your eligibility and issues the certification to those who pass. Atlantis prepares candidates; the course has no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: Do Wichita aircraft manufacturers require a CWI?
faq.a: It depends on the employer and the role. Much of an airframe is fastened rather than welded, and aerospace welding inspection follows customer specifications. The CWI is most useful to inspectors at suppliers, tooling shops and ground equipment makers, and to anyone who wants to move between aerospace and industrial work.

faq.q: Which Part C code suits aerospace welding inspection?
faq.a: AWS D17.1, the specification for fusion welding for aerospace applications, is the Part C option closest to that work. If you also inspect tooling or stands built to D1.1, choose the book for the welds you expect to accept most often.

faq.q: I travel to El Dorado refinery turnarounds. Which code should I pick?
faq.a: The ASME option, which pairs Section IX with the B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes. Refinery piping is built and repaired to those documents.

faq.q: Where do Wichita candidates sit the exam?
faq.a: Parts A and C are booked with Prometric using the eligibility code in your AWS confirmation. Part B is held only at AWS seminar and examination locations on dates AWS sets, so it may mean travel to another city.

faq.q: Does a WSU Tech welding degree shorten the experience requirement?
faq.a: It can. AWS lists two years of experience for an associate degree in a qualifying field and four for completed trade courses, against five with a high school diploma. AWS decides whether a particular program qualifies, so include transcripts with your application.

faq.q: Can an aerospace supplier run the six days at its own plant?
faq.a: Yes. Corporate delivery brings the six days to your facility, uses your welded parts, gauges and specification, and can split the code day between D17.1, D1.1 and the ASME book. Request a quote.

faq.q: Can the one-to-one sessions be in person?
faq.a: Yes, at a location agreed when booking, or they can run online. All six days are one-to-one with the instructor and follow the course outline.

faq.q: Are the practice questions copied from AWS examinations?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes every practice question and timed paper to the subject areas AWS publishes and has no access to the live exam.
